title: The Smart Vehicle and the Factory of the Future
overview: Software, data, electrification and advanced manufacturing in China.

guide.objective: Understand how electrification, software, data and AI interact across vehicle architecture and factory operations.
procedure: Read each slide and state a prediction before changing any parameter.
Run the balanced baseline scenario and record output, rejects, work in process and OEE.
Change one parameter at a time: supply interval, buffer capacity or reliability.
Repeat with the same random seed, compare scenarios and explain the bottleneck.
Export the results and distinguish model output from external evidence.
guide.model: A discrete-event production line runs for 480 simulated minutes in 0.25-minute steps. Stations have cycle times, finite buffers, failures, repairs and quality rejects. Hourly reliability r is converted to a per-step failure probability: 1 − r^(Δt/60). Seed 20261115 makes runs reproducible. Ideal station capacity is 60 / cycle time (units per hour). Line OEE is an educational approximation based on the bottleneck station.
guide.limitations: The model discretizes time and is not calibrated to a real factory. The AI-factory scenario changes assumed parameters; it does not establish a causal effect of AI. Work in process includes queues and units being processed. Lost supply is recorded separately. OEE is not an audited BYD or industry metric.
questions: What happens when a station that is not the bottleneck becomes faster?
How much does predictive maintenance improve final good output?
What changes when buffer capacity is reduced?
Can OEE rise while the number of conforming vehicles falls?
guide.answers: Speeding up a non-bottleneck station may not increase final throughput. Buffers absorb variation but cannot remove a persistent capacity constraint. A technology investment matters only when it changes the binding constraint or reduces losses at the relevant stage.

slides.title: The Smart Vehicle and the Factory of the Future
slides.subtitle: Software, data and advanced manufacturing in China.
items: Architecture, driver assistance and over-the-air updates.
Robotics, quality control and production capacity.
slides.takeaway: How do these technologies work together to create value?
slides.notes: Opening slide. Frame the vehicle and the factory as connected digital and physical systems. The economic result depends on coordination across hardware, software, data, suppliers and production operations.

slides.title: Four Industrial Transformations
slides.subtitle: Competitiveness depends on their integration.
items: Battery, power electronics, motor and charging.
Centralized or zonal computing, applications and OTA updates.
Perception, maintenance, planning and product improvement.
Robotics, logistics, traceability and quality control.
slides.takeaway: An isolated improvement can simply move the bottleneck.
slides.notes: Explain that these four transformations are complements. A better battery, faster software or faster robot does not guarantee higher system output if another stage constrains the process.

slides.title: The Software-Defined Vehicle
slides.subtitle: A conceptual architecture with updateable functions.
items: Sensors, actuators, battery and computing units.
Operating system, communications and separation of safety-critical functions.
Driver assistance, cockpit and services, each requiring specific validation.
Remote distribution with version management and cybersecurity.
slides.takeaway: Remote updates require safety validation throughout the vehicle life cycle.
slides.notes: Not every vehicle uses a single computer. Centralized and zonal architectures are alternative design choices. An application must not be able to compromise safety-critical functions. OTA updates require rollback, cybersecurity and validation.

slides.title: Huawei in the Automotive Ecosystem
slides.subtitle: A technology and platform supplier.
items: Sensors, perception, planning and control, depending on vehicle and version.
Data and updates subject to privacy and security requirements.
slides.takeaway: Distinguish the technology supplier, the vehicle manufacturer and the operator.
slides.notes: Use Huawei as an example of a technology supplier within a broader ecosystem. Do not conflate the supplier's role with the automaker's legal and operational responsibilities.

slides.title: Assistance, Automation and Responsibility
slides.subtitle: SAE levels are defined by the task and the operational domain.
items: The driver supervises the environment and remains responsible for driving.
The system performs the driving task within its domain and may request intervention.
The system handles fallback within its operational domain.
Automation in all road conditions that a human driver could manage.
slides.takeaway: A commercial name does not establish the level of automation.
slides.notes: Correct a common misconception: the driver is not permanently responsible in every level. Level 4 can operate within a limited operational design domain; it is not universal autonomy.

slides.title: The Factory as a Production System
slides.subtitle: The laboratory represents serial stations with finite buffers.
items: 60 / cycle time in minutes = units per hour.
Ideal cycle time × total units / operating time.
slides.takeaway: OEE = A × P × Q. Actual output also depends on supply and buffers.
slides.notes: Use conventional OEE definitions. In the laboratory, OEE is an approximate line indicator based on the bottleneck station, not empirical data from BYD. Distinguish local station efficiency from end-to-end throughput.

slides.title: Value Chains and Geoeconomics
slides.subtitle: Costs and capabilities are distributed across sectors.
items: Electric grid, charging, standards and trade.
slides.takeaway: For Latin America, identify concrete capabilities before inferring opportunities.
slides.notes: Treat regional opportunities as hypotheses for specialization, not forecasts of investment or employment. Ask which local suppliers, skills and institutions could occupy specific value-chain segments.

slides.title: Summary and Experiment
slides.subtitle: A faster factory can still produce fewer good units.
items: Run the baseline and AI-factory scenarios with the same random seed.
Change buffer capacity, supply or reliability.
Record good units, rejects, WIP and OEE.
Identify whether the constraint is processing, supply or quality.
slides.takeaway: What changes when you optimize a station that is not the bottleneck?
slides.notes: The model parameters are synthetic. Have students explain the mechanism behind the observed result rather than merely reporting which scenario produced the largest number.
